disclaimer: This library is general education, not a diagnosis or a treatment plan. Timelines are typical ranges and yours may differ. If anything in a red-flag list applies, or you are not clearly improving within two weeks, see a physiotherapist or sports doctor before you go back on the mat.

mat_levels.solo: Solo movement and rehab on the mat. No partner contact.
mat_levels.drill: Cooperative drilling with a trusted partner. No resistance.
mat_levels.positional: Positional sparring from safe positions at 50-70%.
mat_levels.light: Flow rolling and light rounds with chosen partners.

sources.title: Hinz et al. 2021, Injury patterns, risk factors and return to sport in Brazilian jiu-jitsu (Orthop J Sports Med)
McDonald et al. 2017, Prevalence of injuries during Brazilian jiu-jitsu training (Sports)
Kreiswirth et al. 2014, Incidence of injury among male BJJ fighters at the World No-Gi Championship (J Athl Train)
Prevalence and profile of musculoskeletal injuries in high-performance BJJ athletes
University of Delaware / Sanford Health MCL sprain rehabilitation guidelines
Consensus statement on concussion in sport, Amsterdam 2022 (graduated return to sport)

injuries.name: MCL Sprain
injuries.tagline: Inner-knee ligament. The most commonly injured knee ligament in BJJ.
how: Knee forced inward while the foot is trapped: knee-cut passes, someone falling on the outside of your leg, tangled takedowns
Twisting out of half guard or a leg entanglement
Forcing a sweep with the knee collapsed in
symptoms: Pain on the inner side of the knee, sore to press
Pain when the knee is pushed inward or when you squeeze your knees together
Mild swelling and stiffness; the knee may feel loose in worse sprains
red_flags: A pop followed by fast swelling within hours
The knee gives way or will not straighten fully (locking)
You cannot put weight on it
Clear looseness when the knee is pushed sideways

phases.name: Calm it down

work.name: Quad sets (press knee into a towel)

progress_when: Walking without a limp
Swelling is going down
Knee bends past 110 degrees

phases.name: Rebuild strength
progress_when: Full, pain-free bend and straighten
Single-leg squat to a chair without the knee caving in
No swelling the day after exercise

phases.name: Load and side-to-side
goals: Tolerance to sideways and twisting load

work.name: Split squats or lunges, add weight

progress_when: Hop and land on the injured leg without pain
Side lunges are pain-free
Drilling causes no pain during or the next morning

phases.name: Return to rolling
goals: Positional rounds, then light rolls, then everything

work.name: Add guard play with partners you trust

progress_when: Two weeks of full drilling with no flare-up
Strength within about 10% of the other leg
You are not guarding the knee when you roll

avoid: Knee-cut passing on the injured side early on
Half guard bottom with the injured leg trapped
Leg entanglements and heel hook exchanges
Triangles and closed guard squeezing in the first weeks
prevent: Tap to knee pressure early; knees give no warning
Strengthen adductors and hamstrings (Copenhagen planks, Nordic curls)
Do not spin against a trapped foot
Keep the weight of big partners off the outside of a planted leg

injuries.name: Meniscus Irritation or Tear
injuries.tagline: The knee's shock-absorbing cartilage. Hates deep bending plus twisting.
how: Deep knee bend with rotation: lotus-style guards, rubber guard, sitting back on your heels
Twisting on a planted foot in a scramble
Heel hooks and toe holds that rotate the shin
symptoms: Pain along the joint line, inner or outer
Swelling that builds over a day
Catching, clicking or a feeling that something is in the way
Pain at the end of a deep squat
red_flags: Knee locks and will not straighten
Knee gives way repeatedly
Large swelling within hours of the injury
No improvement after 4-6 weeks of sensible rehab

phases.name: Settle the joint

work.name: Heel props to regain full extension
Quad sets and straight leg raises

progress_when: Knee straightens fully
Little or no swelling
Walking normally

phases.name: Strength without twisting
goals: Leg strength in a pain-free range
No deep flexion under load yet
progress_when: Squat to 90 degrees with load, no pain
No catching or swelling after sessions
Single-leg balance for 45 s

phases.name: Depth and rotation
progress_when: Full squat without pain or catching
Hopping and landing are comfortable
Cooperative drilling causes no next-day swelling

phases.name: Return to rolling
goals: Rounds with controlled partners, building to full

work.name: Reintroduce your guards one at a time

progress_when: A month of training with no swelling or locking

avoid: Sitting on your heels and seiza
Rubber guard, lotus and deep De La Riva hooks
Inverting under pressure
Any rotational leg lock exchange
prevent: Do not force flexibility your hips do not have; the knee pays for it
Build hip rotation so the knee is not asked to twist
Tap early to toe holds and heel hooks
Keep leg strength up year-round

injuries.name: ACL or LCL Injury
injuries.tagline: The serious ones. Usually a pop, fast swelling and an unstable knee.
how: Heel hooks and reaping forces applied fast or not tapped to
Takedowns that load a planted, twisted leg
A partner landing across the knee
symptoms: A pop at the moment of injury
Swelling within a few hours
The knee feels unstable or shifts when you turn
LCL: pain and looseness on the outer side
red_flags: Every suspected ACL or LCL injury needs a clinical exam and usually imaging
Numbness, tingling or a cold foot is an emergency
The knee buckles when walking

phases.name: Get assessed
goals: Diagnosis from a sports doctor or physio
progress_when: You have a diagnosis and a plan
Knee straightens fully
Swelling is under control

phases.name: Supervised strengthening
goals: Quad and hamstring strength, normal walking

work.name: Upper-body and core training that keeps the knee quiet

progress_when: Cleared by your clinician for running and agility

phases.name: Sport preparation
goals: Strength within 10% of the other leg
Jumping, landing and change of direction
progress_when: Passed strength and hop testing
Cleared for contact by your clinician

phases.name: Graded return
goals: Drilling, then positional, then selected rolls
progress_when: Full training without swelling, pain or instability

avoid: Any rolling until cleared
Leg entanglements for a long time after return
Jumping guard, yours or anyone's onto you
prevent: Tap to heel hooks on position, not on pain
Never jump guard and do not let partners jump on you
Hamstring and hip strength: Nordic curls, single-leg deadlifts
Learn to fall and concede takedowns

injuries.name: AC Joint Sprain
injuries.tagline: The bump on top of the shoulder. Usually from landing on it.
how: Falling straight onto the point of the shoulder in a takedown or sweep
Being stacked or driven shoulder-first into the mat
Posting on an outstretched arm
symptoms: Pain right on top of the shoulder
A visible step or bump in worse sprains
Pain reaching across your chest or lifting overhead
Painful to lie on that side
red_flags: Obvious deformity or a large step at the collarbone
Numbness or weakness down the arm
Could not lift the arm at all after the fall

phases.name: Protect
goals: Keep elbow, wrist and neck moving

work.name: Grip and elbow range of motion

progress_when: Resting pain is gone
Arm lifts to shoulder height

phases.name: Range and control

work.name: Band external rotation, elbow at side

progress_when: Full overhead reach
Can reach across the chest with little pain

phases.name: Strength
progress_when: Ten pain-free push-ups
Can take weight on a posted arm
Breakfalls on that side do not hurt

phases.name: Return to rolling
progress_when: Full training including takedowns with no pain the next day

avoid: Takedown rounds and judo throws
Being stacked
Shoulder pressure from north-south and cross-face on that side
prevent: Drill breakfalls until they are automatic
Do not post a straight arm when you are thrown
Build shoulder and upper-back strength

injuries.name: Rotator Cuff Strain
injuries.tagline: The small muscles that hold the shoulder in its socket. Kimura territory.
how: Kimuras, americanas and omoplatas tapped to late
Posting or framing with the arm away from the body under heavy load
Repeated overhead gripping and pulling
symptoms: Deep ache in the shoulder or outer upper arm
Pain lifting the arm out to the side or rotating it
Pain lying on that shoulder at night
Weakness reaching behind your back
red_flags: Sudden inability to lift the arm after an injury
Pain at night that is not easing after two weeks
Marked weakness compared with the other side
Numbness or tingling down the arm

phases.name: Settle
goals: Reduce irritation without freezing the shoulder

work.name: Isometric external and internal rotation into a wall

progress_when: Night pain is easing
Arm lifts to shoulder height comfortably

phases.name: Cuff strength
progress_when: Full range without a painful arc
Rotation strength close to the other side

phases.name: Load the shoulder
progress_when: Overhead press and hanging are pain-free
Drilling causes no ache that night

phases.name: Return to rolling
goals: Rolling with an agreement on shoulder locks

work.name: Rounds where partners catch and release kimuras

progress_when: Full rounds with no pain after

avoid: Fighting kimuras and americanas with the arm away from your body
Stiff-arm frames under heavy top pressure
Overhead lifting through pain
prevent: Tap to shoulder locks early; they tear before they hurt much
Frame with forearms and structure, not a pushing arm
Two short sets of band external rotations before training

injuries.name: Shoulder Subluxation or Dislocation
injuries.tagline: The joint slipped part-way or all the way out. Take this one seriously.
how: Arm forced up and back: posting behind you, whizzer fights, armdrags resisted badly
Kimura with the elbow lifted away
Falling on an outstretched arm
symptoms: A feeling of the shoulder sliding out and back in
Dead-arm sensation
Fear or pain with the arm up and rotated out
Dislocation: obvious deformity and severe pain
red_flags: A shoulder that stays out needs emergency care; do not let a team-mate put it back
A first dislocation needs imaging
Numbness over the outer shoulder or weakness lifting the arm
Repeated episodes: see an orthopaedic specialist

phases.name: Protect and assess
goals: Rest in a sling if advised

work.name: Grip squeezes, elbow and wrist movement
Gentle isometrics with the arm at your side

progress_when: Cleared to start moving the shoulder
Resting pain is gone

phases.name: Controlled range
goals: Regain range without stressing the front of the joint
progress_when: Near-full range below shoulder height
No feeling of slipping in daily life

phases.name: Stability strength
goals: Strong cuff and shoulder blade muscles
progress_when: No apprehension with the arm up and out
Strength close to the other side

phases.name: Graded contact
progress_when: Full training with no slipping and no fear

avoid: Posting an arm behind you
Whizzer and overhook battles on that side
Fighting kimuras
Overhead pressing behind the neck
prevent: Keep elbows close; arms away from the body are levers for your partner
Year-round cuff and shoulder blade strength
Tap as soon as the arm is isolated behind you

injuries.name: Elbow Hyperextension (Armbar Elbow)
injuries.tagline: The armbar you tapped to late.
how: Armbars finished fast or resisted too long
Posting a straight arm when falling
Getting stacked on a locked arm
symptoms: Pain at the front or inner side of the elbow
Cannot fully straighten or bend without pain
Swelling and stiffness the next morning
Weak, sore grip
red_flags: A pop with immediate swelling or bruising
The elbow feels loose or shifts
Numbness or tingling in the ring and little fingers
Cannot straighten after two weeks

phases.name: Settle
goals: Gentle movement inside the pain-free range

work.name: Elbow bend and straighten, short of pain
Forearm rotation, palm up and down

progress_when: Swelling is down
Nearly full bend and straighten

phases.name: Strengthen in mid-range
goals: Biceps, triceps and forearm strength without end-range stress
progress_when: Full range with only mild end-range discomfort
Daily tasks are pain-free

phases.name: Load the lock-out

work.name: Cooperative drilling, no armbars on that side

progress_when: Push-ups and hanging are pain-free
Grip strength is back

phases.name: Return to rolling

work.name: Rounds where you tap to any armbar position

progress_when: Full training with no ache the next day

avoid: Posting on a straight arm
Armbar escapes that rely on resisting the extension
Heavy grip fighting early on
prevent: Tap when the arm is isolated and your thumb turns up, not when it hurts
Keep elbows bent and tight to your ribs
Learn the hitchhiker and stack escapes so you stop holding on with strength

injuries.name: Grappler's Elbow (Tendon Overload)
injuries.tagline: Golfer's or tennis elbow from thousands of grips.
how: Gi gripping volume: collar, sleeve and pant grips held too long
Lots of pulling without enough recovery
A sudden jump in training volume
symptoms: Ache on the inner (golfer's) or outer (tennis) bony point of the elbow
Pain when gripping, opening jars or shaking hands
Stiff and sore in the morning, warms up, then aches after
red_flags: Numbness or tingling into the hand
Elbow locking or sudden sharp pain with a pop
Pain at rest that does not ease after a few weeks of reduced gripping

phases.name: Reduce the load
goals: Cut gripping volume, not all training

work.name: Isometric wrist flexion or extension holds
No-gi or grip-light rounds instead of gi gripping

progress_when: Morning pain 3/10 or less
Isometric holds are comfortable

phases.name: Slow heavy loading
goals: Tendon capacity through slow, heavy work
progress_when: Loaded exercises are 3/10 pain or less and settle within a day
Grip strength is returning

phases.name: Back to full gripping

work.name: Add gi rounds back one at a time

progress_when: A normal week of gi training with no next-day flare

avoid: Death grips you refuse to let go of
Back-to-back gi days with heavy grip fighting
Complete rest; tendons need load to heal
prevent: Let go of grips that are lost
Mix gi and no-gi across the week
Train finger and wrist extensors as well as flexors
Increase weekly mat time by small steps

injuries.name: Finger Sprain (Gi Fingers)
injuries.tagline: Jammed, twisted and swollen knuckles from gripping.
how: Fingers caught in the gi when a partner rips a grip free
Jamming a finger on the mat or a partner
Years of hard pistol and spider grips
symptoms: Swollen, stiff middle knuckle
Pain gripping or making a fist
Tender on the side of the joint
red_flags: The finger is crooked or will not straighten
You cannot bend or straighten the fingertip on its own
Numbness in the finger
Severe swelling and bruising right after injury

phases.name: Protect
progress_when: Swelling is going down
You can nearly make a full fist

phases.name: Restore grip
progress_when: Full fist
Gripping a gi is uncomfortable but not painful

phases.name: Full gripping
goals: Back to gi gripping, taped as needed

work.name: Tape the joint for gi sessions

progress_when: Gi rounds do not flare the joint

avoid: Spider and lasso guards while it is swollen
Hanging on to grips being stripped
Cracking or yanking the finger
prevent: Release grips before they are ripped out
Tape vulnerable joints for gi training
Keep fingers together when posting
Train finger extensors

injuries.name: Wrist Sprain
injuries.tagline: From posting on a bent-back hand or a wrist lock.
how: Catching your weight on an outstretched hand
Wrist locks tapped to late
Collapsing on a posted hand during a sweep
symptoms: Pain bending the wrist back or loading it
Swelling over the back or thumb side
Weak, painful grip
red_flags: Pain in the hollow at the base of the thumb; scaphoid fractures are easy to miss
Obvious deformity or severe swelling
Numbness or tingling in the fingers
Not improving after two weeks

phases.name: Settle

work.name: Support with tape or a brace

progress_when: Swelling is down
Most of your range is back

phases.name: Strength

work.name: Radial and ulnar deviation with a hammer

progress_when: Full range
Grip close to the other side

phases.name: Weight-bearing
goals: Posting and pushing through the hand
progress_when: Push-ups and posting are pain-free

avoid: Posting on a flat hand; use a fist or forearm
Wrist-lock exchanges
Push-ups on palms early
prevent: Post on your forearm or elbow when swept
Strengthen wrists in all directions
Tap to wrist locks at once; they come on fast

injuries.name: Neck Strain
how: Being stacked while defending triangles or playing inverted guard
Guillotines, can-openers and neck cranks
Bridging on your head; driving in with a bad takedown posture
symptoms: Stiff, sore neck, worse turning or looking down
Muscle spasm into the shoulders
A headache at the base of the skull
red_flags: Numbness, tingling or weakness in an arm or hand
Pain shooting down the arm
Severe pain after a fall or hard crank, especially in the midline
Dizziness, double vision, trouble swallowing or loss of balance
Any loss of bladder or bowel control: emergency

phases.name: Keep it moving

work.name: Gentle rotations and side bends in the pain-free range

progress_when: Turning the head is at least 75% of normal
No arm symptoms

phases.name: Isometric strength
goals: Neck strength in all directions without movement

work.name: Isometric holds against your hand: front, back, both sides
Chin tuck with head lift, lying down

progress_when: Full, pain-free range
Isometrics feel strong and symmetrical

phases.name: Load and drilling

work.name: Front and back bridges with hand support

progress_when: Drilling causes no stiffness the next day

phases.name: Return to rolling
goals: Rolling with no stacking and no neck attacks at first
progress_when: Full rounds with no symptoms

avoid: Inverting and being stacked
Fighting guillotines with your neck instead of your hands and posture
Bridging on your head
Shooting takedowns with your head down
prevent: Train the neck directly twice a week
Tap to neck cranks; they are not toughness tests
When stacked, turn onto a shoulder and get your hips back down
Head up, back straight on every shot

injuries.name: Lower Back Strain
injuries.tagline: From stacking, lifting people and living in rounded positions.
how: Being stacked or folded in guard
Lifting a partner with a rounded back to break guard or finish a takedown
Long periods rounded in closed guard or turtle
Twisting under load
symptoms: Ache or tightness across the lower back
Spasm and stiffness, worse in the morning or after sitting
Pain bending forward or arching back
red_flags: Pain, numbness or tingling below the knee
Weakness in a leg or a foot that drags
Numbness around the groin or saddle area, or any change in bladder or bowel control: emergency
Pain after a heavy fall, or constant night pain

phases.name: Stay moving
goals: Walk; do not lie in bed

work.name: Lying knee rocks side to side
Prone press-ups if they feel good

progress_when: Walking and sitting are comfortable
You can bend to put on socks

phases.name: Core endurance

work.name: Hip flexor and hip rotation stretches

progress_when: Core work is pain-free
Forward bend is close to normal

phases.name: Hinge and lift
progress_when: Lifting and drilling leave no next-day stiffness

phases.name: Return to rolling
goals: Top positions first, guard and standing later
progress_when: A normal training week with no flare

avoid: Being stacked; open your guard instead of holding on
Standing guard breaks with a rounded back
Deep inversions
Long drives right after hard sessions without moving around
prevent: Hinge at the hips when you lift anyone
Core endurance work twice a week
Keep hips mobile so the back does not have to round
Warm up properly before rolling

injuries.name: Rib or Rib-Cartilage Injury
injuries.tagline: The popped rib. Hurts to breathe, laugh and train.
how: Knee-on-belly and heavy pressure on the ribcage
Twisting hard under a pin or during a scramble
A knee or elbow landing on your side
Body triangles squeezed across the floating ribs
symptoms: Sharp, pin-point pain at the side or front of the ribcage
Worse with deep breaths, coughing, sneezing, twisting or sitting up
Sometimes a pop or click at the time
Tender to press
red_flags: Shortness of breath or breathing that is getting harder
Coughing blood
Severe pain after a heavy impact
Fever or a cough that develops afterwards
Pain in the lower left ribs with left shoulder-tip pain

phases.name: Breathe and wait

work.name: Slow deep breaths to full expansion
Sleep propped up if lying flat hurts

progress_when: Deep breaths and coughing are tolerable
You can get out of bed without bracing

phases.name: Gentle movement
progress_when: Rotation and side-bending are nearly pain-free
No pain with a sneeze

phases.name: Core and drilling
progress_when: Sit-ups and shrimping are pain-free
Pressing on the spot is only mildly tender

phases.name: Return to rolling

work.name: Full rolling
work.dose: when pressure on the ribs is fine

progress_when: You can take knee-on-belly without pain

avoid: Any bottom position under pressure until late
Rolling with much heavier partners
Coming back early; re-injury restarts the clock
Strapping the chest tightly for days
prevent: Frame early so pressure never settles on your ribs
Do not twist explosively under a heavy pin
Tap to body triangles and crushing pressure
Trunk rotation strength: Pallof presses, side planks

injuries.name: Ankle Sprain
injuries.tagline: Rolled in a scramble or caught in a foot lock.
how: Rolling the ankle while standing, in takedowns or on mat edges
Straight ankle locks and toe holds tapped to late
A foot caught under you when sitting back
symptoms: Pain and swelling on the outer ankle, sometimes bruising
Hurts to walk or push off
Stiff and weak; may feel unstable
red_flags: You cannot take four steps
Tender on the bone at the back edge of either ankle bone or the outer midfoot
Obvious deformity
Numbness in the foot
Pain high above the ankle between the shin bones

phases.name: Settle and move
progress_when: Walking with little or no limp
Swelling is going down

phases.name: Strength and balance

work.name: Calf raises, two legs then one
Single-leg balance, eyes open then closed

progress_when: 20 single-leg calf raises
Balance for 30 s with eyes closed

phases.name: Dynamic

work.name: Drilling, tape the ankle if it helps

progress_when: Single-leg hops are pain-free and feel stable

phases.name: Return to rolling
goals: Ground first, then standing; foot locks last
progress_when: Standing rounds with no pain or giving way

avoid: Takedown rounds until hopping is solid
Foot lock exchanges on that leg
Sitting back on your heels
Stopping rehab when the pain goes; balance is what prevents the next one
prevent: Keep doing single-leg balance work
Tap to ankle locks early and do not spin against toe holds
Watch mat gaps and edges
Strong calves

injuries.name: Toe Sprain (Turf Toe)
injuries.tagline: Big toe bent back too far or caught in the mat.
how: Driving off the toes in a shot or pass with the toe bent back
Toes catching on the mat or in a gi
A partner landing on your heel while your toes are planted
symptoms: Pain and swelling at the base of the big toe
Hurts to push off, sprint or kneel on your toes
Stiff joint
red_flags: Toe looks out of place
You cannot put weight on the forefoot
Heavy bruising under the toe
Not improving after 2-3 weeks

phases.name: Protect

work.name: Tape the big toe to limit backward bend

progress_when: Walking is comfortable
Swelling is going down

phases.name: Mobility and strength
progress_when: Calf raises on that foot are pain-free
Kneeling on your toes is tolerable

phases.name: Push-off
progress_when: Driving off the toe is pain-free

avoid: Combat base and shots on that foot early
Passing on your toes
Training untaped
prevent: Keep toes active, not dragging, when you move
Tape toes that have been injured before
Calf and foot strength

injuries.name: Groin or Hip Flexor Strain
injuries.tagline: From squeezing guards, wide bases and being split open.
how: Squeezing closed guard or triangles hard for a long time
Legs forced apart: banana split, leg drags, wide base in passing
Explosive bridging or shooting without a warm-up
symptoms: Pain high on the inner thigh or at the front of the hip
Hurts to squeeze the knees together or lift the knee
Tight and sore after sitting
red_flags: A pop with bruising down the inner thigh
Deep groin pain with clicking or locking of the hip
Pain with coughing or sneezing low in the abdomen
Not improving after 3-4 weeks

phases.name: Settle

work.name: Isometric ball squeeze between the knees, gentle

progress_when: Walking and stairs are pain-free
A gentle squeeze does not hurt

phases.name: Strengthen
goals: Adductor and hip flexor strength through range
progress_when: A hard squeeze is pain-free
Side lunges are comfortable

phases.name: Load and drill
progress_when: Drilling and full-range stretches are pain-free

phases.name: Return to rolling
goals: Rolling without closed guard at first

work.name: Rounds using open and half guard

progress_when: Full squeezing is pain-free the next day

avoid: Holding closed guard or triangles with strength
Aggressive stretching in the first two weeks
Explosive shots
prevent: Copenhagen planks once or twice a week all year
Warm the hips up before rolling
Open your guard and move instead of clamping

injuries.name: Cauliflower Ear (Fresh)
injuries.tagline: A soft, swollen ear is a 48-hour problem. Act fast.
how: Friction and shearing: escaping headlocks, triangles and guillotines by pulling your head out
Cross-face and head pressure
Direct knocks to the ear
symptoms: A soft, squishy, warm swelling on the outer ear
Tender and throbbing
The ear's folds look puffed out
red_flags: Any fresh fluid-filled swelling: get it drained by a clinician within 24-48 hours, then compressed, or it hardens for good
Increasing redness, heat, pus or fever
Hearing change or severe pain

phases.name: Drain and compress
goals: Keep it compressed so it does not refill

work.name: Compression: clinician's dressing or ear magnets

progress_when: No refilling for 3-4 days
No sign of infection

phases.name: Protected training
goals: Train without friction on the ear

work.name: Wear ear guards for every session
Drilling and positional work, no head squeezing

progress_when: Ear is flat, firm and not tender

phases.name: Back to rolling
goals: Full rolling with ear guards while it settles

work.name: Keep ear guards on for hard rounds

progress_when: No swelling after hard rounds

avoid: Draining it yourself; infection in ear cartilage is serious
Rolling while it is filled or freshly drained
Ripping your head out of chokes and triangles
prevent: Wear ear guards when your ears are sore
Escape with posture and angle, not by yanking your head free
Ice a sore ear right after training

injuries.name: Skin Infection (Ringworm, Staph, Herpes)
injuries.tagline: Not an injury, but the most common reason to stay off the mat.
how: Skin-to-skin contact with an infected partner
Dirty mats, unwashed gear, shared towels
Small cuts and mat burns that let bacteria in
symptoms: Ringworm: red, scaly, itchy ring with a clearer centre
Staph or impetigo: red, warm, painful bump or boil, or honey-coloured crusts
Herpes gladiatorum: a cluster of small painful blisters, often on the face or neck, sometimes with fever
red_flags: A hot, spreading red area, red streaks or fever: see a doctor the same day
A boil that is growing or very painful
Blisters near the eye
Anything that has not improved after a week of treatment

phases.name: Off the mat, get treated

work.name: See a doctor or pharmacist; do not guess
Wash all gear hot; disinfect bags and belts
Strength, conditioning and solo study at home

progress_when: Ringworm: at least 72 hours of antifungal treatment and the patch is clearly healing
Bacterial: at least 72 hours of antibiotics, no new lesions for 48 hours, nothing moist or draining
Herpes: all blisters dry and firmly crusted, on antiviral treatment as prescribed, no new blisters for 72 hours

phases.name: Return
goals: Back to training without spreading it

work.name: Finish the full course of treatment
Cover healing patches if your coach asks

progress_when: Skin fully healed

avoid: Training with it covered up and hoping
Sharing towels, razors or gear
Stopping treatment when it looks better
prevent: Shower straight after every session
Fresh, clean gi or rashguard every time
Cover cuts and mat burns
Check your skin weekly and speak up early
Do not walk barefoot off the mat and back on

injuries.name: Concussion
injuries.tagline: A brain injury. No toughing it out.
how: Head hitting the mat in a takedown or throw
Accidental knee, elbow or head clash in a scramble
Being slammed
symptoms: Headache or pressure in the head
Dizziness, balance problems, nausea
Fogginess, slow thinking, poor memory of the event
Sensitivity to light or noise
Unusual tiredness, irritability or poor sleep
red_flags: Go to emergency care for: loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, a worsening headache, seizure, confusion that is increasing, slurred speech, weakness or numbness, unequal pupils, neck pain
Any suspected concussion: stop training that day and see a doctor
Symptoms lasting more than two weeks need specialist review

phases.name: Relative rest
goals: Rest body and brain; limit screens, no alcohol

work.name: Normal daily activity that does not worsen symptoms

progress_when: Symptoms are settling
